paragraphs: Web agents combine language models with the ability to act on websites, making security failures potentially consequential when they can access sensitive resources. AdvAgent studies these vulnerabilities through automated red-teaming: deliberately challenging an agent to discover where its behavior can be manipulated. Its black-box setting uses feedback from the target agent to develop attacks.

The framework trains an adversarial prompting model through reinforcement learning. Instead of relying only on fixed attack prompts, it uses the target agent’s responses to improve the prompts it generates. The attack design also aims to preserve stealthiness and controllability, making these properties part of the framework’s objectives alongside attack effectiveness.

Evaluations report high attack success against GPT-4-based web agents across varied web tasks. The authors also find that existing prompt-based defenses offer limited protection against these attacks. Together, these results show that the tested agents remain vulnerable even when such defenses are present, motivating stronger protections for agents whose outputs can trigger actions.
icml-2025-advagent-controllable-blackbox.tldr: AdvAgent learns adversarial prompts from black-box feedback and exposes weaknesses in GPT-4-based web agents and their prompt-based defenses.

paragraphs: Aguvis addresses the challenge of making an autonomous agent operate graphical interfaces across platforms. Existing approaches can depend on textual descriptions of interfaces, platform-specific actions, and limited planning capabilities. The proposed framework works directly from screen images and standardizes interactions, bringing visual understanding and task execution into a common approach.

The authors build a large dataset containing annotations for both visual grounding and reasoning. Grounding connects an intended interaction to the relevant part of the screen, while planning determines how actions contribute to the larger task. Aguvis separates these capabilities into two training stages and incorporates structured reasoning through an inner monologue.

Experiments report state-of-the-art performance on both offline benchmarks and real-world online evaluations. The authors also describe Aguvis as the first fully autonomous vision-based GUI agent to operate without closed-source models. Releasing its datasets, models, and training recipes makes the framework available for further research into agents that interpret interfaces visually and carry out tasks.
icml-2025-aguvis-unified-pure-vision-age.tldr: Aguvis combines screen-based interaction, visual grounding, and structured planning in an open-source autonomous GUI agent.

paragraphs: CoastalBench provides a dataset for learning to emulate coastal circulation, a setting where detailed numerical simulations can be expensive. The paper identifies limited training and validation data as an obstacle to developing deep learning alternatives, particularly when the goal is to represent complex processes at high spatial resolution.

The dataset covers a decade of simulated coastal conditions in southwest Florida. It uses a real-world three-dimensional mesh with around six million cells and spatial resolution finer than 100 meters. Recorded quantities include water velocities, surface level, temperature, and salinity, together with atmospheric and river inputs that influence coastal behavior.

The authors evaluate a customized Vision Transformer that predicts ocean variables at different lead times from initial conditions, boundary conditions, and external forcings. The central contribution is a shared resource for testing models on detailed coastal simulations. Its combination of geometry, evolving ocean variables, and external drivers creates opportunities to benchmark approaches such as physics-informed learning and neural operators.
icml-2025-coastalbench-a-decade-long-hig.tldr: CoastalBench supplies a decade of detailed coastal simulations to support training and evaluation of machine learning emulators.

paragraphs: CogReact studies how to model human cognitive responses when environmental influences change over time. Such changes can make the relationship between a stimulus and a person’s behavior difficult to identify. The paper argues that models developed mainly under ideal conditions miss an important part of this problem: disturbances that affect cognition as it unfolds.

The proposed framework combines drift-diffusion modeling with deep reinforcement learning. This combination is used to represent detailed effects of dynamic stimuli on cognitive processing. A central feature is attention to when environmental inputs occur, allowing their temporal influence to contribute to the model’s account of behavior.

Across different cognitive tasks and environmental influences, the authors report improved quantitative modeling and the ability to capture differences associated with both individual subjects and particular stimuli. They also report qualitative agreement with general trends in cognitive responses. The contribution is a data-driven way to simulate behavior under changing conditions while accounting for variation across people and environmental inputs.
icml-2025-cogreact-a-reinforced-framewor.tldr: CogReact combines drift-diffusion modeling and reinforcement learning to simulate human cognitive responses to changing environmental stimuli.

paragraphs: Contradiction retrieval searches for documents that disagree with a query, a useful capability for fact checking and cleaning datasets. The challenge is to identify explicit disagreement while preserving the subtle meanings that distinguish opposing statements. SparseCL addresses limitations the authors identify in similarity search and cross-encoder approaches.

The method trains sentence embeddings to retain distinctions relevant to contradiction. It then combines cosine similarity with a sparsity function to score candidate documents. This makes retrieval depend on a richer relationship than similarity alone, while allowing the central comparisons to be performed through vector calculations rather than exhaustive document comparisons.

Experiments on Arguana, MSMARCO, and HotpotQA report an average improvement of 11.0% across different models. The authors also evaluate downstream uses in natural language inference and cleaning corrupted text collections. These findings support the idea that embeddings can be designed around a specific semantic relationship, making contradiction retrieval both more effective and computationally efficient in the evaluated settings.
icml-2025-contradiction-retrieval-via-co.tldr: SparseCL combines contradiction-aware sentence embeddings with similarity and sparsity scoring to retrieve opposing documents efficiently.

paragraphs: The Heterogeneous Data Game examines markets where multiple machine learning providers compete to serve different data sources. This changes the modeling question: a provider’s choice depends on competitors as well as the diversity of the data. The paper develops a game-theoretic framework to analyze these interactions.

Its main object of study is a pure Nash equilibrium, a configuration in which no provider benefits by changing its choice alone. The analysis shows that such equilibria may fail to exist. When they do exist, providers may all choose the same model or specialize in distinct data sources, producing homogeneous or heterogeneous outcomes.

The authors study markets with one provider, two providers, and more general configurations. They identify the temperature parameter in data-source choice models and the dominance of particular sources as factors shaping equilibrium behavior. The results offer a theoretical account of when competition can encourage convergence or specialization, with implications for strategies and regulatory thinking about machine learning marketplaces.
icml-2025-heterogeneous-data-game-charac.tldr: A game-theoretic framework shows how competition across diverse data sources can produce model convergence, specialization, or no pure equilibrium.

paragraphs: Transferring a classifier between modalities can involve two changes at once: inputs use different representations, and class labels occur at different frequencies. The paper introduces Heterogeneous Label Shift to study this combined problem. Its motivation is that addressing only one part leaves important difficulties in cross-modal knowledge transfer unresolved.

The authors first analyze how feature-space differences and changes in label distributions affect generalization. They derive an error decomposition theorem, providing a theoretical way to separate contributions to prediction error. This separation then guides a learning framework that minimizes a bound while handling feature heterogeneity and label shift as distinct components.

Experiments across cross-modal classification benchmarks support the effectiveness of the proposed approach. The main significance is the connection between the theoretical decomposition and the algorithm’s organization: the method explicitly accounts for both differences in how inputs are represented and differences in class prevalence. This provides a coordinated treatment of two shifts that occur together in the setting studied.
icml-2025-heterogeneous-label-shift-theo.tldr: Heterogeneous Label Shift jointly addresses changing input representations and class distributions through an error decomposition and bound-minimization framework.

paragraphs: Using a language model to judge pairs of answers can produce rankings of instruction-following systems. But comparisons against a single baseline depend critically on preferences behaving transitively: if one system is preferred to a second and that second to a third, the ordering should remain consistent. This paper investigates that assumption within AlpacaEval.

The authors find non-transitive preferences in LLM judges and show that model rankings can change with the selected baseline. They mitigate this by combining round-robin comparisons with Bradley-Terry preference models. Comparing systems across a broader set of opponents gives the ranking process more information than comparisons centered on one baseline.

The resulting rankings align more closely with Chatbot Arena: Spearman correlation rises from 95.0% to 96.4%, and Kendall correlation from 82.1% to 86.3%. Because round-robin evaluation is computationally costly, the authors also propose Swim tournaments. Their dynamic matchmaking strategy aims to retain the benefits of broader comparisons while making the evaluation process more efficient.
icml-2025-investigating-non-transitivity.tldr: LLM judges exhibit non-transitive preferences, and tournament-based comparisons produce rankings less dependent on a single baseline.

paragraphs: This paper investigates an attention mechanism associated with language models’ ability to learn from examples in their context. Its starting point is induction heads, which the abstract describes as a cornerstone of this ability and as requiring at least two attention layers. The authors ask whether this mechanism can be supported more efficiently.

They propose KV shifting attention and provide a theoretical proof that it reduces the induction-head mechanism’s dependence on model depth and width. The contribution therefore concerns how much architectural capacity is needed to support induction. It connects a change in attention to an analysis of the mechanism that the change is intended to improve.

Experiments report improved learning of induction heads together with better language modeling. The reported benefits take the form of superior performance or faster convergence, across settings ranging from toy models to pretrained models exceeding ten billion parameters. These results connect the theoretical motivation to observed training and modeling benefits across substantially different model scales.
icml-2025-kv-shifting-attention-enhances.tldr: KV shifting attention reduces architectural demands on induction mechanisms and improves language modeling performance or convergence in experiments.

paragraphs: Task-Aware Learngene, or TAL, focuses on choosing useful starting parameters for models before training. The paper builds on parameter prediction with Graph HyperNetworks, which it identifies as struggling with larger models, smaller datasets, and the need to train a separate initializer for each task. These difficulties increase computational and storage costs.

TAL first learns under the guidance of an already trained model. It then undergoes multi-task tuning to produce a shared initializer. This model predicts parameters using both the architecture being initialized and the characteristics of the target task, bringing structural and task information into the same parameter-generation process.

Experiments report that models initialized with TAL outperform those initialized with GHN by an average of 24.39% in accuracy across Decathlon datasets. The result supports the usefulness of a shared, task-aware initialization model in the evaluated setting. More broadly, the approach makes adaptation part of parameter prediction, addressing the overhead associated with maintaining separate task-specific initializers.
icml-2025-learngene-tells-you-how-to-cus.tldr: TAL learns a shared initializer that predicts model parameters from architecture and task information, outperforming GHN initialization on Decathlon datasets.

paragraphs: Contextual bandits learn which actions to choose using observed context and rewards. When several units act in the same round, one unit’s action can also affect another unit’s reward. This interference complicates reward estimation because outcomes depend on interactions among choices as well as the choice made for a particular unit.

The paper develops a framework for incorporating interference into linear contextual bandits. Its algorithms explicitly quantify interference when modeling rewards, connecting a concept from causal inference with sequential decision-making. The aim is to account for these cross-unit effects when estimating expected rewards and choosing actions.

The authors provide theoretical guarantees that include sublinear regret, finite-sample upper bounds, and asymptotic properties. Sublinear regret describes a setting where accumulated decision loss grows more slowly than the decision horizon. Simulations and synthetic data generated using MovieLens support the approach’s effectiveness. Together, the theory and experiments establish a way to study online learning when the consequences of actions extend across units.
icml-2025-linear-contextual-bandits-with.tldr: This framework extends linear contextual bandits to model cross-unit effects of actions and provides theoretical and simulation-based support.

paragraphs: MDDM hides messages within the process of generating images with diffusion models. The paper targets practical difficulties in earlier generative steganography methods, including accurate message recovery and control over the resulting image. Its approach allows the message to influence image generation while users retain the ability to guide image content through prompts.

The framework uses a Cardan grille to encode a message into Gaussian noise, which becomes the starting input for diffusion-based generation. It does not require additional training. During recovery, the receiver uses the pre-shared grille and diffusion inversion to recover the message without needing the original generation prompt or random seed.

Experiments report advantages in recovery accuracy, controllability, practicality, and security. With suitable strategies and settings, message-recovery accuracy can approach 100%; the claim is explicitly conditional on those settings. The authors also report some robustness and potential use in watermarking. The practical contribution is a generation-and-recovery workflow that reduces what sender and receiver must share.
icml-2025-mddm-practical-message-driven-.tldr: MDDM encodes messages into diffusion-model noise and recovers them using a shared grille, with near-perfect accuracy under appropriate settings.

paragraphs: Glycans are built from sugar units, but representing only how those units connect leaves out their internal atomic structure. The paper argues that this missing detail matters for predicting glycan properties. GlycanAA therefore represents both the larger sugar-unit backbone and the atoms that make up each unit.

The model uses a heterogeneous graph with separate node types for monosaccharides and atoms. Hierarchical message passing connects information from local atomic interactions to interactions across the larger backbone. This gives the model a way to combine details at different structural scales within a single glycan representation.

The authors also pretrain the model on a high-quality unlabeled glycan dataset, producing PreGlycanAA. A multi-scale masking task teaches it to predict hidden information and learn dependencies at different levels. Benchmark results show GlycanAA outperforming existing glycan encoders, with further improvements from pretraining. The findings support both including atomic detail and learning structural relationships from unlabeled glycans before downstream use.
icml-2025-modeling-all-atom-glycan-struc.tldr: GlycanAA combines atom-level and sugar-unit graphs, while multi-scale pretraining further improves its glycan representations.

paragraphs: Looped Transformers repeatedly apply a Transformer computation, offering benefits in parameter efficiency and reasoning. This paper investigates their ability to approximate sequence-to-sequence functions. The central question is how the looped architecture affects the accuracy with which it can represent a desired mapping between input and output sequences.

The authors establish an approximation rate using a modulus of continuity, which characterizes how a function’s outputs change when its inputs change. Their analysis reveals a limitation specific to the looped architecture. That finding motivates adding scaling parameters for each loop, with those parameters conditioned on an encoding of the current timestep.

The modification gives successive iterations information about their position in the repeated computation. Experiments support the theoretical analysis: increasing the number of loops improves performance, and timestep encoding produces further gains. The paper thus connects an expressiveness analysis to an architectural enhancement, showing empirical benefits from both additional iterations and making the repeated computation sensitive to the iteration index.
icml-2025-on-expressive-power-of-looped-.tldr: An approximation analysis motivates timestep-conditioned scaling in looped Transformers, which improves performance in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: ProSec aims to make code-generating language models follow secure coding practices. Earlier approaches collect examples from real vulnerabilities, but the paper identifies limited data availability and poor fit with modern multi-stage post-training workflows as obstacles. ProSec addresses these issues by actively creating security-relevant training situations.

The method synthesizes coding scenarios from Common Weakness Enumerations to expose vulnerabilities in a model’s generated code. It then produces fixes for vulnerable snippets and uses preference-learning objectives to teach the model secure practices. This links training examples to weaknesses elicited from the model itself, providing a systematic way to build security-focused alignment data.

The synthesized scenarios elicit 25 times more vulnerable code than a normal instruction-tuning dataset, yielding a security-focused dataset seven times larger than previous work. Experiments report models that are 25.2% to 35.4% more secure than previous work without reduced utility. These findings support proactive scenario generation as a way to expand security training while preserving useful code-generation capabilities.
icml-2025-prosec-fortifying-code-llms-wi.tldr: ProSec generates vulnerability-inducing coding tasks and fixes to improve code-model security through preference learning without reported utility loss.

paragraphs: RE-IMAGINE addresses a problem in evaluating language-model reasoning: strong benchmark scores may partly reflect recall of training material. The framework organizes reasoning ability into a hierarchy inspired by associations, interventions, and counterfactuals. It pairs that hierarchy with an automated method for generating related problems at different levels.

The key technique is to alter problems in an intermediate symbolic representation. This enables the framework to generate arbitrarily many variations that cannot be solved through memorization alone. Because the changes operate on a symbolic form, the approach is designed to work across domains such as mathematics, code, and logic.

The authors apply the framework to four widely used benchmarks and evaluate several model families. Performance decreases when models receive the generated variations. These results indicate that statistical recall contributes to earlier benchmark performance, without establishing that all successful answers arise from recall. The contribution is a scalable way to probe how reasoning performance holds up when familiar problems undergo structured changes.
icml-2025-re-imagine-symbolic-benchmark-.tldr: RE-IMAGINE generates symbolic problem variations that reveal a degree of reliance on statistical recall in reasoning-benchmark performance.

paragraphs: This paper sharpens theoretical guarantees for two neural approaches to solving partial differential equations: the Deep Ritz Method and physics-informed neural networks. Generalization analysis concerns how well learning from sampled information controls error beyond those samples. The contribution is a more refined mathematical treatment for specified classes of elliptic equations.

For the Deep Ritz Method, the authors study the Poisson and static Schrödinger equations on a d-dimensional unit hypercube with Neumann boundary conditions. They use localization techniques to obtain sharper bounds, assuming the exact solutions belong to Barron spaces or general Sobolev spaces. These solution-space assumptions define the scope of the analysis.

For physics-informed neural networks, the paper considers general linear second-order elliptic equations with Dirichlet boundary conditions. It uses local Rademacher complexity in a multi-task learning formulation to analyze generalization. The authors additionally discuss over-parameterized models when solutions belong to Barron space. The results strengthen error analysis for these neural solvers under the stated equation, boundary, and solution assumptions.
icml-2025-refined-generalization-analysi.tldr: The paper derives sharper generalization bounds for neural PDE solvers under specified boundary conditions and assumptions about solution spaces.

paragraphs: RePaViT targets feedforward layers as a major source of Vision Transformer inference latency. The authors find that these layers contribute more latency than attention layers, with their impact growing as models become larger. This finding motivates changing the feedforward computation to make it easier to simplify after training.

The proposed channel-idle mechanism lets some feature channels bypass the nonlinear activation in each feedforward layer. Those channels form a linear pathway, enabling structural reparameterization for inference. The resulting model can therefore use a reorganized computation at testing time, with the design providing the structure needed for that transformation.

Across evaluated Vision Transformers, the method reduces latency with accuracy tradeoffs that improve as model size increases. Under the same training strategy, RePa-ViT-Large and RePa-ViT-Huge achieve reported speedups of 66.8% and 68.7%, alongside top-1 accuracy improvements of 1.7% and 1.1%. These results indicate that the efficiency benefits can coexist with accuracy gains, particularly in the larger models studied.
icml-2025-repavit-scalable-vision-transf.tldr: RePaViT creates linear pathways in feedforward layers that enable faster inference, with particularly strong results in larger Vision Transformers.

paragraphs: ResKoopNet studies nonlinear dynamical systems through the Koopman operator, a framework that provides a linear representation useful for analyzing complex behavior. Approximating its spectral components remains difficult, especially in high-dimensional settings. The paper focuses on a limitation of methods that assess and filter spectral candidates only after those candidates have been computed.

Residual Dynamic Mode Decomposition uses a spectral residual to measure approximation accuracy, but filtering a precomputed spectrum cannot recover information absent from that initial set. ResKoopNet instead explicitly minimizes the residual when computing Koopman eigenpairs. Neural networks make this residual part of the learning process, enabling a more precise and complete spectral approximation.

The authors provide theoretical guarantees and evaluate the method on physical and biological systems. Experiments show more accurate spectral approximations than existing methods, particularly for high-dimensional systems and systems with continuous spectra. The key methodological change is to use an approximation-quality measure to guide discovery directly, expanding its role beyond checking previously generated spectral estimates.
icml-2025-reskoopnet-learning-koopman-re.tldr: ResKoopNet directly minimizes spectral residuals to learn more accurate Koopman spectral representations of complex dynamical systems.

paragraphs: Model merging combines capabilities from multiple fine-tuned models, but the combined model can lose performance when little task data is available. This paper first establishes a worst-case result: merging algorithms that ignore data can perform arbitrarily badly. The result motivates using domain-specific examples to guide the merging process.

The authors introduce ProDistill, a few-shot method built around progressive layer-wise teacher-student distillation. It connects model merging to learning from the outputs or representations of teacher models. Their findings challenge the expectation that layer-wise training necessarily harms performance: in this setting, the approach improves merging quality while supporting larger-scale models.

Experiments report state-of-the-art performance relative to existing few-shot merging methods, with improvements of up to 6.14% on vision tasks and 6.61% on natural language understanding tasks. Additional experiments include models with more than ten billion parameters. Together, these results support layer-wise distillation as a practical way to combine model capabilities when only a small amount of relevant data is available.
icml-2025-scalable-model-merging-with-pr.tldr: ProDistill uses progressive layer-wise distillation and a few domain examples to improve model merging and scale beyond ten billion parameters.

paragraphs: ConsFormer uses a Transformer to improve candidate assignments for constraint satisfaction problems. Training such models often depends on already having feasible solutions or using reinforcement learning with substantial training costs and carefully designed rewards. The paper develops a self-supervised alternative that learns from the constraints themselves.

The method replaces discrete constraints with differentiable approximations that can guide training. Starting from random assignments, the Transformer learns to make a single improvement step. At test time, that same refinement process is applied repeatedly, constructing a solution through a sequence of updates resembling local search. This separates the length of training updates from the amount of computation used during solving.

Experiments cover Sudoku, graph coloring, nurse rostering, and MAXCUT. The authors report that additional test-time iterations allow the method to tackle out-of-distribution problems. The finding suggests that a learned local improvement rule can remain useful beyond its training distribution when given more opportunities to refine an assignment, without requiring feasible solutions as training labels.
icml-2025-self-supervised-transformers-a.tldr: ConsFormer learns single-step assignment improvements from differentiable constraints and repeatedly applies them to solve problems at test time.

paragraphs: PINNMamba addresses failures in physics-informed neural networks that prevent patterns in initial conditions from propagating through a predicted PDE solution. The authors attribute these failures to two causes: neural networks’ preference for simpler patterns and a mismatch between continuous equations and the discrete samples used for learning.

Their approach introduces sub-sequence modeling with a state space model. The paper identifies state space models as a connection between continuous and discrete representations that allows initial-condition information to propagate. It also argues that aligning sequences at a moderate granularity can eliminate the simplicity bias responsible for the analyzed failure modes.

Experiments report error reductions of up to 86.3% relative to a state-of-the-art architecture. This is a maximum reported improvement across the evaluated settings. The contribution links a diagnosis of information-propagation failures to a sequence-based architecture, showing how the organization of sampled points and their interactions can substantially affect the quality of physics-informed solutions in the tested problems.
icml-2025-sub-sequential-physics-informe.tldr: PINNMamba uses state space sub-sequence modeling to improve initial-condition propagation, reducing PDE-solution errors by up to 86.3% in experiments.

paragraphs: This paper develops a kernel-based approach to solving nonlinear partial differential equations with lower computational overhead. The authors identify a scaling problem in solvers that embed differential operators inside kernels: constructing relationships among solutions and their derivatives becomes complicated as the number of collocation points grows.

The proposed method represents the solution with standard kernel interpolation and computes derivatives by differentiating that interpolant. This avoids the complex Gram matrix construction used by the compared approach. In a particular implementation, grid-based collocation points and a product kernel produce a Kronecker product structure, allowing computation without constructing the full Gram matrix.

The authors prove convergence and analyze its rate under appropriate regularity assumptions. Numerical experiments on several benchmark PDEs demonstrate advantages of the approach. Its significance lies in separating the solution representation from derivative evaluation and then exploiting structured interpolation. The convergence claim depends on the stated regularity conditions, while the described computational shortcut uses the grid and product-kernel structure.
icml-2025-toward-efficient-kernel-based-.tldr: A kernel PDE solver differentiates a standard interpolant and exploits product structure to reduce computation, with convergence under regularity assumptions.

paragraphs: UGPhysics evaluates language models on undergraduate physics reasoning, a domain the authors argue is insufficiently covered by existing benchmarks. The motivation is that success in mathematics does not by itself establish broad physics reasoning ability. The benchmark is designed to examine both the range and depth of that ability.

It contains 5,520 problems in English and Chinese, spanning 13 subjects, seven answer types, and four physics reasoning skills. The problems undergo rigorous screening for data leakage. The authors also develop MARJ, a model-assisted rule-based judging pipeline tailored to assessing physics answers, pairing the problem collection with an evaluation procedure suited to the domain.

Among 31 evaluated language models, the highest overall accuracy is 49.8%, achieved by OpenAI-o1-mini. This result indicates substantial room for improvement on the benchmark’s undergraduate physics tasks. The contribution is therefore both a broad test collection and a specialized assessment pipeline, providing a basis for measuring progress in physics reasoning beyond mathematical problem-solving performance.
icml-2025-ugphysics-a-comprehensive-benc.tldr: UGPhysics tests undergraduate physics reasoning across 5,520 problems, with the best of 31 evaluated models reaching 49.8% accuracy.

paragraphs: XAttention targets the computational cost of attention in long-context Transformers. Block-sparse attention reduces work by concentrating on selected regions of the attention matrix, but deciding which blocks matter can itself be expensive. The paper focuses on making that selection process efficient enough to deliver practical computational savings.

Its central idea is to estimate a block’s importance using the sum of values along its antidiagonal, running from lower left to upper right. This score acts as a proxy for the block’s contribution, allowing the framework to identify and prune less important blocks. XAttention is presented as a plug-and-play approach to sparse attention during inference.

Evaluations include RULER and LongBench for language, VideoMME for video understanding, and VBench for video generation. The authors report accuracy comparable to full attention and up to 13.5-fold acceleration in attention computation. That speedup concerns the attention operation specifically. The results support inexpensive block scoring as a way to make sparse attention effective across several long-context applications.
icml-2025-xattention-block-sparse-attent.tldr: XAttention uses antidiagonal scores to prune attention blocks, achieving comparable accuracy and up to 13.5-fold faster attention computation.
